e.etymology: The Greek form of Hebrew Toviyah, my good is the Lord. Tobias is the young hero of the Book of Tobit, and Toby is its English short form.
From the dahlia flower, named for the 18th-century Swedish botanist Anders Dahl, whose surname means valley. It has been used as a given name since the 19th century.

assoc.t: the Black Dahlia, unsolved 1947 Los Angeles murder

e.etymology: From Sanskrit bodhi, awakening or enlightenment, the state the Buddha reached beneath the Bodhi tree. Its use as an English name is modern, helped along by film characters.

assoc.t: the Bodhi tree where the Buddha reached enlightenment
Bodhi, Patrick Swayze's surfer in Point Break

e.meaning: from the Sierra de Aitana mountains in Spain
e.etymology: From the Sierra de Aitana, a mountain range in eastern Spain. The exiled poet Rafael Alberti first gave it to his daughter in 1941, in memory of his last view of his homeland.
namesakes: Aitana Bonmatí (Spanish soccer star and Ballon d'Or winner)

assoc.t: Aitana, Spanish pop singer

e.meaning: round, stout (old name Cada); or barrel maker
e.etymology: From an English surname with several sources: the old personal name Cada, an occupational name for a cooper from Old French cade, barrel, and a word for a pet animal. It also serves as a short form of Caden.
Borrowed in the Middle Ages from a Low German and Dutch short form of Theodoric, from Germanic words for people and ruler. It was revived in the 19th century.
namesakes: Derek Jeter (Yankees Hall of Fame shortstop)
Derek Hough (Dancing with the Stars dancer and judge)

e.etymology: From the English word reign, a monarch's rule, from Old French reigne and Latin regnum, kingdom. It took off as a given name in the 2010s.

assoc.t: Reign energy drinks from Monster Beverage

e.etymology: From Hebrew lilit, a night spirit, a word with older Mesopotamian roots. In Jewish folklore Lilith is Adam's first wife, who refused to obey him and left Eden.

assoc.t: Adam's first wife in Jewish folklore, later a demon
Lilith Sternin, Frasier's ex-wife on Cheers and Frasier
Lilith Fair, 1990s women's music festival
Lilith, demon villain of the game Diablo IV

e.note: In Jewish folklore Lilith is a night demon who preys on infants, so some religious families find the name unsettling.

e.meaning: son of Hendrick, a form of Henry
e.etymology: A spelling of the surname Hendricks, son of Hendrick, the Dutch and Low German form of Henry. Its use as a first name follows the fame of guitarist Jimi Hendrix.

assoc.t: Jimi Hendrix, rock guitar legend

e.meaning: short form of Jackson, son of Jack
e.etymology: A clipped form of Jackson or Jaxon, or a stylized spelling of the surname Jacks. The x ending took off in the 2010s alongside Jaxon and Dax.

assoc.t: Jax Teller, biker lead of Sons of Anarchy
Jax, common nickname for Jacksonville, Florida
Jax, fighter in the Mortal Kombat games

e.meaning: form of Helen, often read as shining light
e.etymology: A modern variant of Elaine written the way Elena sounds. Elaine is the Old French form of Helen and the name of several women in Arthurian legend.
A K spelling of Caden, a name coined in the United States in the 1990s that rhymes with Aiden, Braden and Jaden.
From the capital of England, Old English Lunden, from Roman Londinium, a name of Celtic origin. It is also a surname for someone who came from the city.
namesakes: Jack London (author of The Call of the Wild)

assoc.t: the capital of England and the United Kingdom

e.meaning: archer, from the Dutch surname Cuyler
e.etymology: From a rare American surname, an anglicized form of Dutch Cuyler and German Keiler. As a first name since the 1980s it may simply be a blend of Kyle and Tyler.

e.meaning: broad island or broad eye; in Ireland, descendant of Brádach
e.etymology: From a surname with two sources: Irish O Bradaigh, descendant of Brádach, and an English name from Old English brad, broad, with a word for island or eye.
namesakes: Tom Brady (seven-time Super Bowl champion quarterback)

assoc.t: Tom Brady, NFL quarterback
The Brady Bunch, 1970s TV family sitcom

e.etymology: From Old French Jehanne, a feminine form of John, which goes back to Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. It has been the standard English feminine of John since the 17th century.
namesakes: Jane Austen (author of Pride and Prejudice)

assoc.t: Jane Doe, placeholder name for an unidentified woman
plain Jane, an ordinary-looking woman
Jane, Tarzan's companion
Jane Eyre, Charlotte Brontë's heroine

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of George, from Greek Georgios, from georgos, farmer or earth-worker. Saint George, the dragon-slaying soldier martyr, spread it across Europe.
From Gaelic Mael Coluim, devotee of Saint Columba, the Irish missionary whose name means dove. Four kings of Scotland bore it, including the Malcolm who succeeds Macbeth.
namesakes: Malcolm Gladwell (author of The Tipping Point)

assoc.t: Malcolm X, civil rights leader
Malcolm in the Middle, 2000s sitcom

e.etymology: From the Danish surname Jensen, son of Jens, the Danish form of John. It is among the most common surnames in Denmark.

assoc.t: actor Jensen Ackles and Nvidia chief Jensen Huang

e.etymology: From the Latin word maximus, greatest, a Roman family name and the name of several early saints. The 2000 film Gladiator brought it into modern use.

assoc.t: Maximus, Russell Crowe's general in Gladiator
Maximus, the palace horse in Disney's Tangled

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Maximilian, from the Roman name Maximilianus, a derivative of Maximus, greatest.

From the Anglo-Norman surname de Warenne, after a place on the river Varenne in Normandy, whose name comes from a Gaulish word for water. The English word warren, a game park, is a separate source of the surname.

assoc.t: a rabbit warren, a network of burrows

e.etymology: A short form of the medieval name Amabel, from Latin amabilis, lovable. A favorite around 1900, it has returned to fashion.

assoc.t: Mabel Pines of Disney's Gravity Falls
Mabel Mora, Selena Gomez in Only Murders in the Building

e.etymology: From a surname. Americans know it chiefly from Baylor University in Waco, Texas, named for its co-founder Judge R. E. B. Baylor.
namesakes: Elgin Baylor (NBA Hall of Fame forward)

assoc.t: Baylor University in Waco, Texas

e.etymology: From a surname taken from Kendal in Cumbria, valley of the river Kent. Another place, Kendale, comes from Old Norse kelda, spring, and dalr, valley.
namesakes: Kendall Jenner (model and reality TV star)

assoc.t: Kendall Jenner, model and reality TV star
Kendall-Jackson wines

e.etymology: A Spanish pet form of Dolores, sorrows, from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de los Dolores, Our Lady of Sorrows.

assoc.t: Lola Bunny of Looney Tunes and Space Jam
Lola, 1970 hit song by the Kinks
the showgirl in Barry Manilow's Copacabana
lola, the Tagalog word for grandmother

e.meaning: steward, keeper of the household stores
e.etymology: From an English occupational surname, Middle English spenser, for the servant who ran the spence, the pantry or storeroom of a great house. It is the family name of Princess Diana.

assoc.t: Spencer's, the mall novelty and gag-gift chain
Spencer, 2021 film about Princess Diana

e.etymology: A respelling of London, the English capital, with the y that marks many modern American girls' names such as Jordyn and Brooklyn.

assoc.t: sounds the same as London, the English capital

e.etymology: The French form of Latin Lucilla, a feminine diminutive of Lucius, from lux, light. It was most popular in the US in the 1910s.
namesakes: Lucille Ball (star of I Love Lucy)

assoc.t: Lucille Ball, star of I Love Lucy
Lucille, B.B. King's name for his guitars
Lucille, Negan's barbed-wire bat in The Walking Dead

e.etymology: Made a given name by Princess Leia of Star Wars (1977). It is also treated as a form of the Biblical Leah, which is Leia in Biblical Greek.

assoc.t: Princess Leia of Star Wars

e.meaning: attendant at religious rites (Camilla); also Arabic for perfect
e.etymology: The Polish, Czech and Slovak spelling of Camilla, from a Roman family name linked to camillus, a youth who served at religious rites. Arabic Kamila, the feminine of Kamil, perfect, is a separate name.

e.meaning: uncertain; long linked with Greek kyrios, lord
e.etymology: From Old Persian Kurush through Greek Kyros and Latin Cyrus. Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire in the 6th century BC and appears in the Bible as the king who freed the Jews from Babylon.
namesakes: Cyrus the Great (founder of the Persian Empire)

assoc.t: Miley Cyrus, pop singer, as a surname
Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian Empire
